title: CRDs & Operators
summary: Add your own API types with CustomResourceDefinitions, manage them with kubectl, and automate them with controllers and operators.

blocks.text: The master ledger normally holds familiar forms, like bays. A **custom resource** adds a new kind of form, registered or removed while the port runs, and your radio (`kubectl`) handles it like any other. On its own, the form just sits there. Add a specialist supervisor (custom controller) who acts on it, and you have an operator. Most staff badges (RBAC roles) don't cover new forms, so grant access explicitly.

A **resource** is an API endpoint holding objects of one kind (for example `pods`). A **custom resource** extends the API with a kind that isn't in a default install. It can be registered and removed in a running cluster, and once installed you use it with kubectl like any built-in kind.

items: A custom resource alone just stores and returns structured data.
Add a **custom controller** and you get a real **declarative API**: you declare desired state and the controller keeps the actual state in line.
The **operator pattern** = custom resources + custom controllers, encoding app-specific know-how.

blocks.text: Most RBAC roles don't cover new custom resources (only `cluster-admin` or wildcard rules do). Grant access to them explicitly.

Need new paperwork? Adding a form to the ledger (CRD) takes no programming; the front desk files and serves it. Opening your own side desk behind the front desk (API aggregation) takes code but gives more control. If a bay just reads an existing config file, post an instruction sheet (ConfigMap). Don't fill the ledger with customer data: too many forms can overload it.

rows: No programming; the main API server serves and stores the objects
Needs code: your own API server behind the main one, for more control (storage, version conversion)
For an existing config file format consumed by a Pod as a file or env vars

items: Pick a custom resource when you want kubectl support, `.spec`/`.status`/`.metadata` conventions, and automation that watches the object.
Don't use custom resources as storage for application or end-user data.
Custom resources use storage like ConfigMaps do; too many can overload API server storage.
CRDs always use the API server's own authentication, authorization and audit logging.

sections.heading: Anatomy of a CRD
sections.sourceTitle: Extend the Kubernetes API with CustomResourceDefinitions

blocks.text: Designing a new form means filling in a form about forms (the CRD). Its name must read `<plural>.<group>`, like `crontabs.stable.example.com`. You list versions (exactly one is the filed copy, `storage: true`), a strict layout (structural schema) that trims unknown fields, whether filled forms belong to one yard or the whole port (`scope`), and their names. Then wait a few seconds for `Established`.

apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata:
  name: crontabs.stable.example.com   # <plural>.<group>
spec:
  group: stable.example.com           # REST path /apis/<group>/<version>
  versions:
    - name: v1
      served: true                    # enable/disable this version
      storage: true                   # exactly one storage version
      schema:
        openAPIV3Schema:
          type: object
          properties:
            spec:
              type: object
              properties:
                cronSpec:
                  type: string
                replicas:
                  type: integer
  scope: Namespaced                   # or Cluster
  names:
    plural: crontabs
    singular: crontab
    kind: CronTab
    shortNames:
    - ct

items: `scope` makes the custom objects **Namespaced** or **Cluster**-scoped. The CRD object itself is always non-namespaced.
With `apiextensions.k8s.io/v1` a **structural schema** is mandatory. Unknown fields are **pruned** unless a subtree sets `x-kubernetes-preserve-unknown-fields: true`.
Creating the CRD adds an endpoint such as `/apis/stable.example.com/v1/namespaces/*/crontabs/...`. It can take a few seconds: wait for the `Established` condition.

sections.heading: Working with custom objects
sections.sourceTitle: Extend the Kubernetes API with CustomResourceDefinitions

blocks.text: Once the new form type exists, radio for it by plural, singular or short name: `kubectl get ct`. Closing a yard (namespace) shreds the custom forms filed in it. Delete the form type itself (the CRD) and the front desk closes that counter and shreds every filled copy; recreate it and the drawer starts empty. The published layout also powers `kubectl explain`.

kubectl apply -f resourcedefinition.yaml   # create the CRD
kubectl apply -f my-crontab.yaml           # create a CronTab object
kubectl get crontab                        # plural, singular or short name works
kubectl get ct -o yaml
kubectl delete -f resourcedefinition.yaml  # removes the CRD AND all its objects

items: Resource names in kubectl are case-insensitive.
Deleting a namespace deletes the custom objects in it.
Deleting a CRD removes its REST endpoint and every stored object. Recreating it starts empty.
The published schema powers client-side validation and `kubectl explain` for custom resources.

blocks.text: To inspect a custom resource quickly, use the names from the CRD's `names` block: `kubectl get <plural|singular|shortName>`.

sections.heading: Printer columns, subresources, categories, finalizers
sections.sourceTitle: Extend the Kubernetes API with CustomResourceDefinitions

blocks.text: You can dress up the new form: extra columns on the `kubectl get` printout, a separate status window (`/status`) so normal edits ignore `.status`, a scale dial (`/scale`) so `kubectl scale` works, and a category so `kubectl get all` lists it. **Finalizers** work like checkout slips: a delete only stamps a deletion time, and the form stays until every supervisor removes their slip.

rows: Adds columns (with a jsonPath) to kubectl get output
Groups the resource, e.g. `all`, so `kubectl get all` lists it

blocks.text: kubectl scale --replicas=5 crontabs/<name>   # needs the scale subresource
**Finalizers** act as asynchronous pre-delete hooks. A delete sets `metadata.deletionTimestamp`; the object is removed only when every controller has removed its entry from `metadata.finalizers`.

An operator is a specialist supervisor hired for one kind of form, like a database expert. They follow the same control loop as every supervisor, doing what a human expert would: deploy, back up and restore, upgrade, pick a leader. You hire one by adding the form type plus its controller, often as a standing contract (Deployment). Then you just create or edit forms like `SampleDB`, and the expert does the rest.
**Operators** are API clients that act as controllers for a custom resource. They follow the control loop and automate what a human operator would do for one application.

items: Typical jobs: deploy on demand, back up and restore state, handle upgrades (including schema changes), and pick a leader.
**Deploying**: add the CRD and its controller to the cluster. The controller usually runs outside the control plane, for example as a **Deployment**.
**Using**: create, edit or delete objects of the operator's kind; the operator does the rest.
Build your own with tools such as kubebuilder, Operator Framework, Kopf or Java Operator SDK. Find existing ones on OperatorHub.io.

blocks.text:
kubectl get SampleDB                     # list configured databases
kubectl edit SampleDB/<name>             # change settings; the operator reconciles

flashcards.front: What does a custom controller add to a custom resource?
flashcards.back: A declarative API: it keeps actual state matching the declared desired state.

flashcards.front: Two ways to add custom resources?
flashcards.back: CustomResourceDefinitions (no programming) and API aggregation (your own API server).

flashcards.front: Do existing RBAC roles cover new custom resources?
flashcards.back: Mostly no: only cluster-admin or wildcard rules. Grant access explicitly.

flashcards.front: Required form of a CRD's metadata.name?
How many versions can be the storage version?
Is the CustomResourceDefinition object itself namespaced?
flashcards.back: No. CRDs are non-namespaced and available to all namespaces.
plural, singular, kind, and optionally shortNames (and categories).

flashcards.front: What happens to custom objects when you delete their CRD?
flashcards.back: They're all deleted along with the REST endpoint.

flashcards.front: Which condition shows a new CRD is ready to serve?
What's needed for kubectl scale to work on a custom resource?
flashcards.back: The scale subresource (specReplicasPath, statusReplicasPath) in the CRD.

flashcards.front: Make a custom resource show up in kubectl get all?

flashcards.back: An API client acting as a controller for a custom resource, automating one application's operations.

flashcards.front: Most common way to deploy an operator?
flashcards.back: Add its CRD and its controller to the cluster, often running the controller as a Deployment.

questions.stem: A CRD defines `group: stable.example.com` and `names.plural: crontabs`. What must `metadata.name` be?

options.explanation: The name must be <plural>.<group>.
That's only the group.
That's the kind.
The name uses the plural, not the singular.

questions.stem: Which `spec.scope` values does a CRD accept?

options.explanation: The example comments say: either Namespaced or Cluster.
Those are per-version flags, not scope values.
Those are fields under spec.names.

questions.stem: True or false: A CustomResourceDefinition object lives in a namespace, so each namespace needs its own copy.

options.explanation: CRDs are non-namespaced and available to all namespaces.
Correct: one CRD serves the whole cluster.

questions.stem: With the CronTab CRD (`plural: crontabs`, `singular: crontab`, `shortNames: [ct]`) installed, which commands list CronTab objects? Select 3.

options.explanation: Plural works.

stable is part of the group, not a resource name.

options.text: The REST endpoint is removed and all 20 objects are deleted
options.explanation: The server uninstalls the endpoint and deletes all stored custom objects.

options.text: The objects stay and reappear if you recreate the CRD
options.explanation: A recreated CRD starts empty.

options.text: The delete is refused until the objects are removed
options.explanation: The server uninstalls the endpoint and deletes the stored objects.

questions.stem: In a CRD with two versions, how many can have `storage: true`?

options.explanation: One and only one version must be the storage version.
Only one can be the storage version.

options.text: None; storage is set per object
options.explanation: It's set per version in the CRD.

options.text: Any number, as long as served: true
options.explanation: served and storage are separate flags.

questions.stem: You create a custom object with a field not in the CRD's structural schema. What happens by default?

options.explanation: Unspecified fields are pruned unless x-kubernetes-preserve-unknown-fields: true is set.
Only with x-kubernetes-preserve-unknown-fields: true.
Versions come from the CRD spec.
The CRD schema doesn't change.

options.text: The scale subresource, with specReplicasPath and statusReplicasPath
options.explanation: The /scale subresource lets kubectl scale work on a custom resource.
That only changes kubectl get output.
That groups it for kubectl get all.
Finalizers are pre-delete hooks.

questions.stem: You want `kubectl get` to show a Replicas column for your custom resource. Which CRD field?

options.explanation: Columns are defined server-side with a jsonPath.
That exposes /status.
Short aliases for the resource name.

questions.stem: True or false: A custom object with entries in `metadata.finalizers` is removed as soon as you delete it.

options.explanation: Deletion only sets metadata.deletionTimestamp; the object goes once all finalizers are removed.
Correct: controllers must remove their finalizers first.

questions.stem: Which way of adding custom resources needs no programming?

options.explanation: CRDs are simple and need no programming.
Aggregation needs your own API server.
ConfigMaps don't add new resource types.
Secrets hold sensitive data; they don't add resource types.

questions.stem: A developer with an existing namespace-scoped Role can't list a newly installed custom resource. Why?

options.text: Most RBAC roles don't grant access to new resources unless they use wildcards; access must be granted explicitly
options.explanation: Only cluster-admin or wildcard roles cover it automatically.

options.text: CRDs bypass RBAC and use their own authorization
options.explanation: CRDs use the same authn, authz and auditing as built-in resources.

options.text: Custom resources can't be listed with kubectl
options.explanation: kubectl works with custom resources.

options.text: The CRD must be recreated in that namespace
options.explanation: Not the cause described.

questions.stem: Which describe how an operator is normally deployed and used? Select 2.

options.text: Add the CRD and its controller to the cluster
options.explanation: The most common way to deploy an operator.

options.text: Run the controller, for example as a Deployment, outside the control plane
options.explanation: Stated on the Operator pattern page.

options.text: Change and rebuild Kubernetes' own code to add the operator
options.explanation: Operators extend the cluster without changing Kubernetes code.

options.text: Edit the operator's Pods directly to change app settings
options.explanation: You edit objects of the operator's kind, e.g. kubectl edit SampleDB/<name>.

options.text: A client of the Kubernetes API that acts as a controller for a custom resource
options.explanation: That's the page's definition.

options.text: Code that must be compiled into Kubernetes itself
options.explanation: Operators extend cluster behaviour without modifying Kubernetes code.

options.text: A StatefulSet that runs the database
options.explanation: In the SampleDB example, the operator creates the StatefulSet; it isn't the operator.

options.text: A one-off Job that backs up data
options.explanation: The operator may create backup Pods or Jobs, but it is the controller managing them.
